p2.original: The Housing Bubble and the 2007 Financial Crisis
p2.zh: 住房泡沫与2007年金融危机

p3.original: In 2006, housing equity in the United States peaked at $13 trillion. That means that the market prices of homes, less what was still owed on the loans they used to buy these houses, equaled $13 trillion. This was a very good number, since the equity represented the value of the financial asset most U.S. citizens owned.
p3.zh: 2006年,美国住房股本达到顶峰,达到13万亿美元. 这意味着,住房的市场价格,减去他们用于购买这些住房的贷款的欠款,相当于13万亿美元。这个数字非常好,因为股票代表了美国公民拥有的大部分金融资产的价值。

p4.original: However, by 2008 this number declined to $8.8 trillion, and it plummeted further still in 2009. Combined with the decline in value of other financial assets held by U.S. citizens, by 2010, U.S. homeowners’ wealth had shrunk $14 trillion! This is a staggering result, and it affected millions of lives: people had to alter their retirement, housing, and other important consumption decisions. Just about every other large economy in the world suffered a decline in the market value of financial assets, as a result of the 2008-2009 global financial crisis.
p4.zh: 然而,到2008年,这一数字降至8.8万亿美元,2009年进一步暴跌。加上美国公民持有的其他金融资产价值下降,到2010年,美国房主的财富已经缩水了14万亿美元! 这是一个惊人的结果,它影响到数百万人的生活:人们不得不改变他们的退休、住房和其他重要的消费决定。 由于2008-2009年全球金融危机,世界上大约每个其他大型经济体的金融资产市场价值都有所下降。

p5.original: This chapter will explain why people purchase houses (other than as a place to live), why they buy other types of financial assets, and why businesses sell those financial assets in the first place. The chapter will also give us insight into why financial markets and assets go through boom and bust cycles like the one we described here.
p5.zh: 本章将解释人们为什么购买房屋(而不是作为居住地),为什么购买其他类型的金融资产,以及为什么企业首先出售这些金融资产.本章还将让我们深入了解为什么金融市场和资产会像我们在这里所描述的那样经历繁荣和崩溃的循环。

p11.original: When a firm needs to buy new equipment or build a new facility, it often must go to the financial market to raise funds. Usually firms will add capacity during an economic expansion when profits are on the rise and consumer demand is high. Business investment is one of the critical ingredients needed to sustain economic growth. Even in the sluggish 2009 economy, U.S. firms invested $1.4 trillion in new equipment and structures, in the hope that these investments would generate profits in the years ahead.
p11.zh: 当企业需要购买新设备或建设新设施时,往往必须前往金融市场筹集资金.通常,当利润上升和消费者需求高时,公司将在经济扩张期间增加能力。商业投资是维持经济增长所需的关键要素之一。即使在2009年经济萧条的情况下,美国公司也在新设备和结构方面投资了1.4万亿美元,希望这些投资在未来几年里能够产生利润.

p12.original: Between the end of the recession in 2009 through the second quarter 2013, profits for the S&P 500 companies grew by 9.7% despite the weak economy, with cost cutting and reductions in input costs driving much of that amount, according to the Wall Street Journal.  shows corporate profits after taxes (adjusted for inventory and capital consumption). Despite the steep decline in quarterly net profit in 2008, profits have recovered and surpassed pre-recession levels.
p12.zh: 从2009年衰退结束到2013年第二季度,尽管经济疲软,但S&P 500公司的利润仍增长了9.7%,根据《华尔街日报》,削减成本和减少投入成本驱动了大部分金额。 尽管2008年季度净利润急剧下降,但利润已经恢复并超过了衰退前的水平。

p13.original: Corporate Profits After Tax (Adjusted for Inventory and Capital Consumption)
p13.zh: 公司税后利润(按库存和资本消费调整)

p14.original: Many firms, from huge companies like General Motors to startup firms writing computer software, do not have the financial resources within the firm to make all the desired investments. These firms need financial capital from outside investors, and they are willing to pay interest for the opportunity to obtain a rate of return on the investment of that financial capital.
p14.zh: 许多公司,从通用汽车公司等大型公司到编写计算机软件的创业公司,都不具备公司内部的财政资源来进行所有期望的投资. 这些公司需要外部投资者的金融资本,它们愿意支付利息,以获得该金融资本投资的回报率。

p15.original: On the other side of the financial capital market, financial capital suppliers, like households, wish to use their savings in a way that will provide a return. Individuals cannot, however, take the few thousand dollars that they save in any given year, write a letter to General Motors or some other firm, and negotiate to invest their money with that firm. Financial capital markets bridge this gap: that is, they find ways to take the inflow of funds from many separate financial capital suppliers and transform it into the funds of financial capital demanders desire. Such financial markets include stocks, bonds, bank loans, and other financial investments.
p15.zh: 在金融资本市场的另一边,金融资本供应商与家庭一样,希望以能够提供回报的方式利用他们的储蓄。 然而,个人不能拿他们在特定年份存下的几千美元,写信给通用汽车公司或其他公司,并谈判将其资金投入该公司。金融资本市场弥补了这一差距:即它们找到办法,从许多独立的金融资本供应商那里吸收资金,并将其转化为金融资本需求者所希望的资金。 这种金融市场包括股票、债券、银行贷款和其他金融投资。

p18.original: Our perspective then shifts to consider how these financial investments appear to capital suppliers such as the households that are saving funds. Households have a range of investment options: bank accounts, certificates of deposit, money market mutual funds, bonds, stocks, stock and bond mutual funds, housing, and even tangible assets like gold. Finally, the chapter investigates two methods for becoming rich: a quick and easy method that does not work very well at all, and a slow, reliable method that can work very well over a lifetime.
p18.zh: 然后,我们的观点转向考虑这些金融投资在资本供应商,例如储蓄资金的家庭方面是如何出现的。家庭有一系列投资选择:银行账户、存款证、货币市场共同基金、债券、股票、股票和债券共同基金、住房,甚至黄金等有形资产。 最后,该章研究了两种致富的方法:一种快速而容易的方法完全不起作用,一种缓慢而可靠的方法,在一生中能够非常有效.

p19.zh: 企业如何提高金融资本

p20.original: Firms often make decisions that involve spending money in the present and expecting to earn profits in the future. Examples include when a firm buys a machine that will last 10 years, or builds a new plant that will last for 30 years, or starts a research and development project. Firms can raise the financial capital they need to pay for such projects in four main ways: (1) from early-stage investors; (2) by reinvesting profits; (3) by borrowing through banks or bonds; and (4) by selling stock. When business owners choose financial capital sources, they also choose how to pay for them.
p20.zh: 公司往往作出涉及目前花费资金和预期将来赚取利润的决定。实例包括:公司购买一台将持续10年的机器,或建造一座将持续30年的新工厂,或启动研发项目。公司可以四大方式筹集它们为这类项目支付所需的金融资本:(1) 从早期投资者那里筹集;(2) 通过再投资利润;(3) 通过银行或债券借贷;(4) 通过出售股票。 当企业主选择金融资本来源时,他们也选择如何支付.

p22.original: Firms that are just beginning often have an idea or a prototype for a product or service to sell, but few customers, or even no customers at all, and thus are not earning profits. Such firms face a difficult problem when it comes to raising financial capital: How can a firm that has not yet demonstrated any ability to earn profits pay a rate of return to financial investors?
p22.zh: 刚刚开始的公司往往有一个产品或服务销售的主意或原型,但客户很少,甚至根本没有客户,因此没有赚取利润。此类公司在筹集金融资本方面面临一个困难的问题:一个尚未表现出任何盈利能力的公司如何向金融投资者支付回报率?

p23.original: For many small businesses, the original source of money is the business owner. Someone who decides to start a restaurant or a gas station, for instance, might cover the startup costs by dipping into their own bank account, or by borrowing money (perhaps using a home as collateral). Alternatively, many cities have a network of well-to-do individuals, known as “angel investors,” who will put their own money into small new companies at an early development stage, in exchange for owning some portion of the firm.
p23.zh: 对于许多小企业来说,最初的资金来源是企业主. 例如,决定开办餐馆或加油站的人,可能通过投入自己的银行账户或借钱(也许以住房作为抵押)来支付启动费用。 或者,许多城市都有一个由“天使投资者”组成的好人网络,他们将在早期开发阶段将自己的资金投入到小型的新公司中,以换取拥有公司的一部分。

p24.original: Venture capital firms make financial investments in new companies that are still relatively small in size, but that have potential to grow substantially. These firms gather money from a variety of individual or institutional investors, including banks, institutions like college endowments, insurance companies that hold financial reserves, and corporate pension funds. Venture capital firms do more than just supply money to small startups. They also provide advice on potential products, customers, and key employees. Typically, a venture capital fund invests in a number of firms, and then investors in that fund receive returns according to how the fund as a whole performs.
p24.zh: 风险资本公司对规模仍然相对较小但有大幅增长潜力的新公司进行金融投资。 这些公司从各种个人或机构投资者那里筹集资金,包括银行、大学捐赠机构、持有财务储备金的保险公司以及公司养恤基金。风险资本公司不仅向小型创业企业提供资金。 他们还就潜在的产品、客户和主要雇员提供咨询。通常,风险资本基金投资于一些公司,然后根据基金的整体运作情况向基金投资者收取回报。

p25.original: The amount of money invested in venture capital fluctuates substantially from year to year: as one example, venture capital firms invested more than $48.3 billion in 2014, according to the National Venture Capital Association. All early-stage investors realize that the majority of small startup businesses will never hit it big; many of them will go out of business within a few months or years. They also know that getting in on the ground floor of a few huge successes like a Netflix or an Amazon.com can make up for   multiple failures. Therefore, early-stage investors are willing to take large risks in order to position themselves to gain substantial returns on their investment.
p25.zh: 风险资本投资金额每年波动很大:例如,根据国家风险资本协会,2014年风险资本公司投资超过483亿美元。 所有早期的投资者都意识到,大多数小型创业企业永远不会大打出手;其中许多企业将在几个月或几年内退出企业。 他们也知道,进入Netflix或Amazon.com等几个巨大成功的底层可以弥补多重失败. 因此,早期阶段的投资者愿意承担巨大风险,以便自己能够从投资中获得可观的回报。

p26.original: Profits as a Source of Financial Capital
p26.zh: 作为金融资本来源的利润

p27.original: If firms are earning profits (their revenues are greater than costs), they can choose to reinvest some of these profits in equipment, structures, and research and development. For many established companies, reinvesting their own profits is one primary source of financial capital. Companies and firms just getting started may have numerous attractive investment opportunities, but few current profits to invest. Even large firms can experience a year or two of earning low profits or even suffering losses, but unless the firm can find a steady and reliable financial capital source so that it can continue making real investments in tough times, the firm may not survive until better times arrive. Firms often need to find financial capital sources other than profits.
p27.zh: 如果公司在赚取利润(其收入大于成本),它们可以选择将这些利润中的部分重新投资于设备、结构和研究与开发。 对许多已成立的公司来说,重新投资自己的利润是金融资本的主要来源之一。刚刚开始的公司和公司可能有许多有吸引力的投资机会,但目前投资的利润很少。即使是大公司也可能经历一年两年的低利润,甚至遭受损失,但除非公司能够找到稳定可靠的金融资本来源,以便能在艰难时期继续进行真正的投资,否则公司可能要到更好的时代才能生存下来.企业往往需要找到利润以外的金融资本来源。

p29.original: When a firm has a record of at least earning significant revenues, and better still of earning profits, the firm can make a credible promise to pay interest, and so it becomes possible for the firm to borrow money. Firms have two main borrowing methods: banks and bonds.
p29.zh: 当一家公司至少有赚取大量收入的记录,而且更能赚取利润时,公司可以作出支付利息的可信承诺,因此公司可以借钱.公司主要有两种借贷方法:银行和债券。

p30.original: A bank loan for a firm works in much the same way as a loan for an individual who is buying a car or a house. The firm borrows an amount of money and then promises to repay it, including some rate of interest, over a predetermined period of time. If the firm fails to make its loan payments, the bank (or banks) can often take the firm to court and require it to sell its buildings or equipment to make the loan payments.
p30.zh: 为公司提供的银行贷款与为购买汽车或房屋的个人提供的贷款大同小异。公司借了一笔钱,然后承诺在预先确定的时间内偿还,包括一定的利率。 如果公司未能支付贷款,银行(或银行)往往可以将公司告上法庭,要求其出售其建筑物或设备以支付贷款。

p31.original: Another source of financial capital is a bond. A bond is a financial contract: a borrower agrees to repay the amount that it borrowed and also an interest rate over a period of time in the future. A corporate bond is issued by firms, but bonds are also issued by various levels of government. For example, a municipal bond is issued by cities, a state bond by U.S. states, and a Treasury bond by the federal government through the U.S. Department of the Treasury. A bond specifies an amount that one will borrow, the interest rate that one will pay, and the time until repayment.
p31.zh: 金融资本的另一个来源是债券。债券是金融合同:借款人同意偿还其借入的金额,并在未来一段时间内还本付息.公司债券由公司发行,但债券也由各级政府发行. 例如,城市发行市债券,美国各州发行州债券,联邦政府通过美国发行国库债券.财政部.债券规定将借贷的金额、将支付的利率和偿还期限。

p32.original: A large company, for example, might issue bonds for $10 million. The firm promises to make interest payments at an annual rate of 8%, or $800,000 per year and then, after 10 years, will repay the $10 million it originally borrowed. When a firm issues bonds, it may choose to issue many bonds in smaller amounts that together reach the total amount it wishes to raise. A firm that seeks to borrow $50 million by issuing bonds, might actually issue 10,000 bonds of $5,000 each. In this way, an individual investor could, in effect, loan the firm $5,000, or any multiple of that amount. Anyone who owns a bond and receives the interest payments is called a bondholder. If a firm issues bonds and fails to make the promised interest payments, the bondholders can take the firm to court and require it to pay, even if the firm needs to raise the money by selling buildings or equipment. However, there is no guarantee the firm will have sufficient assets to pay off the bonds. The bondholders may recoup only a portion of what they loaned the firm.
p32.zh: 例如,一家大公司可能以1 000万美元发行债券。公司承诺按8%的年利率支付利息,即每年80万美元,然后在10年后,将偿还它原先借来的1000万美元。公司发行债券时,可以选择发行数额较小,合在一起达到其希望筹集的总金额的众多债券.一家试图通过发行债券借贷5 000万美元的公司实际上可能发行10 000份债券,每份5 000美元。 这样,个人投资者实际上可以向公司贷款5 000美元,或其中任何一笔数额的倍数。持有债券并收取利息的,称为债券持有人.企业发行债券,未按期支付利息的,即使企业需要通过出售建筑物或设备筹集资金,债券持有人也可以将公司告上法庭并要求其支付. 然而,没有保证公司有足够的资产来偿付这些债券。债券持有人只能收回他们借给公司的一部分款项。

p33.original: Bank borrowing is more customized than issuing bonds, so it often works better for relatively small firms. The bank can get to know the firm extremely well—often because the bank can monitor sales and expenses quite accurately by looking at deposits and withdrawals. Relatively large and well-known firms often issue bonds instead. They use bonds to raise new financial capital that pays for investments, or to raise capital to pay off old bonds, or to buy other firms. However, the idea that firms or individuals use banks for relatively smaller loans and bonds for larger loans is not an ironclad rule: sometimes groups of banks make large loans and sometimes relatively small and lesser-known firms issue bonds.
p33.zh: 银行借款比发行债券更符合客户要求,因此往往对相对小型的公司更有效.银行能够非常了解这家公司,这常常是因为银行能够通过观察存款和提款来相当准确地监测销售和开支。相对大型和知名的公司往往发行债券。 他们利用债券筹集支付投资的新金融资本,或者筹集资本来偿还旧债券,或者购买其他公司. 然而,公司或个人利用银行获得较小的贷款和债券获得较大贷款的想法并不是一条铁定的规则:有时银行集团提供大额贷款,有时还发行较小和不太知名的公司债券。

p35.original: A corporation is a business that “incorporates”—that is owned by shareholders that have limited liability for the company's debt but share in its profits (and losses). Corporations may be private or public, and may or may not have publicly traded stock. They may raise funds to finance their operations or new investments by raising capital through selling stock or issuing bonds.
p35.zh: 公司是“公司化”的企业,由对公司债务负有有限责任但分享其利润(和损失)的股东拥有。公司可以是私营的,也可以是公营的,可能拥有也可能没有公开交易的股票。 它们可通过出售股票或发行债券来筹集资金,为业务或新投资提供资金。

p36.original: Those who buy the stock become the firm's owners, or shareholders. Stock represents firm ownership; that is, a person who owns 100% of a company’s stock, by definition, owns the entire company. The company's stock is divided into shares. Corporate giants like IBM, AT&T, Ford, General Electric, Microsoft, Merck, and Exxon all have millions of stock shares. In most large and well-known firms, no individual owns a majority of the stock shares. Instead, large numbers of shareholders—even those who hold thousands of shares—each have only a small slice of the firm's overall ownership.
p36.zh: 购买股票的人成为公司的所有人,或股东。股票代表公司所有权;即按定义拥有100%公司股票的人拥有整个公司。公司股票分为股份.IBM,AT&T,福特,通用电气,微软,默克,埃克森等企业巨头都拥有数百万股股权. 在大多数大型和知名的公司中,没有个人拥有大多数股票。 相反,大量股东——即使是持有数千股股份的股东——各自只有公司总所有权的一小部分。

p37.original:
When a large number of shareholders own a company, there are three questions to ask:
                    
How and when does the company obtain money from its sale of stock?
What rate of return does the company promise to pay when it sells stock?
Who makes decisions in a company owned by a large number of shareholders?
p37.zh: 当大量股东拥有一家公司时,有三个问题要问:公司如何以及何时从股票的销售中获得资金?公司出售股票时承诺支付多少回报率?. 谁在一大批股东拥有的公司中做决定?

p38.original: First, a firm receives money from the stock sale only when the company sells its own stock to the public (the public includes individuals, mutual funds, insurance companies, and pension funds). We call a firm’s first stock sale to the public an initial public offering (IPO). The IPO is important for two reasons. For one, the IPO, and any stock issued thereafter, such as stock held as treasury stock (shares that a company keeps in their own treasury) or new stock issued later as a secondary offering, provides the funds to repay the early-stage investors, like the angel investors and the venture capital firms. A venture capital firm may have a 40% ownership in the firm. When the firm sells stock, the venture capital firm sells its part ownership of the firm to the public. A second reason for the importance of the IPO is that it provides the established company with financial capital for substantially expanding its operations.
p38.zh: 第一,公司只有在公司向公众出售自己的股票(公众包括个人、共同基金、保险公司和养恤基金)时,才能从股票销售中获得资金。 我们称公司首次向公众出售股票是首次公开出售。IPO之所以重要,有两个原因. 其中一种是IPO,以及此后发行的任何股票,如作为国库股票持有的股票(公司在自己的国库中持有的股份),或后来作为次级报价发行的新股票,提供偿还早期投资者的资金,如天使投资者和风险资本公司.风险投资公司可能对公司拥有40%的所有权。企业出售股票时,风险投资公司将其对公司的部分所有权出售给公众.IPO重要性的第二个原因是它为已成立的公司提供了金融资本,以大幅度扩展其业务.

p39.original: However, most of the time when one buys and sells corporate stock the firm receives no financial return at all. If you buy General Motors stock, you almost certainly buy it from the current share owner, and General Motors does not receive any of your money. This pattern should not seem particularly odd. After all, if you buy a house, the current owner receives your money, not the original house builder. Similarly, when you buy stock shares, you are buying a small slice of the firm's ownership from the existing owner—and the firm that originally issued the stock is not a part of this transaction.
p39.zh: 然而,在购买和出售公司股票时,公司大部分时间都得不到任何财务回报。 如果你买通用汽车的股票, 你几乎肯定从现在的股份所有者那里买的, 通用汽车公司不收任何你的钱。 这种模式不应显得特别奇怪。毕竟,如果买房子,现在的房主会收到你的钱,而不是原来的房屋建造者. 同样,在购买股票时,你正在从现有所有者手中购买公司所有权的一小部分——而最初发行股票的公司不属于这一交易的一部分。

p40.original: Second, when a firm decides to issue stock, it must recognize that investors will expect to receive a rate of return. That rate of return can come in two forms. A firm can make a direct payment to its shareholders, called a dividend. Alternatively, a financial investor might buy a share of stock in Wal-Mart for $45 and then later sell it to someone else for $60, for $15 gain. We call the increase in the stock value (or of any asset) between when one buys and sells it a capital gain.
p40.zh: 第二,当一家公司决定发行股票时,它必须承认投资者会期望得到一定的回报率. 这种回报率可以有两种形式。公司可以直接向股东支付,称为红利. 或者,金融投资人可能以45美元的价格购买沃尔玛的股票份额,然后以60美元的价格卖给他人,以获得15美元的收益。 我们称在购买和出售之间增加股票价值(或任何资产)为资本收益。

p41.original: Third: Who makes the decisions about when a firm will issue stock, or pay dividends, or re-invest profits? To understand the answers to these questions, it is useful to separate firms into two groups: private and public.
p41.zh: 第三:由谁决定公司何时发行股票、支付股利或再投资利润? 为了了解这些问题的答案,将公司分为两类是有用的:私营和公营。

p42.original: A private company is frequently owned by the people who generally run it on a day-to-day basis. Individuals can run a private company. We call this a sole proprietorship. If a group runs it, we call it a partnership. A private company can also be a corporation, but with no publicly issued stock. A small law firm run by one person, even if it employs some other lawyers, would be a sole proprietorship. Partners may jointly own a larger law firm. Most private companies are relatively small, but there are some large private corporations, with tens of billions of dollars in annual sales, that do not have publicly issued stock, such as farm products dealer Cargill, the Mars candy company, and the Bechtel engineering and construction firm.
p42.zh: 私人公司经常为一般日常经营的人所拥有.个人可以经营一家私营公司。 我们称之为独资企业。 如果一个团体经营它,我们称之为伙伴关系。私人公司也可以是公司,但没有公开发行的股票。由一人经营的一家小型律师事务所即使雇用了其他律师,也将成为独资公司。合伙人可以共同拥有一个较大的律师事务所. 大多数私营公司相对较小,但有一些大型私营公司,年销售额达数百亿美元,没有公开发行股票,如农产品经销商Cargill,火星糖果公司,以及Bechtel工程和建筑公司.

p43.original: When a firm decides to sell stock, which financial investors can buy and sell, we call it a public company. Shareholders own a public company. Since the shareholders are a very broad group, often consisting of thousands or even millions of investors, the shareholders vote for a board of directors, who in turn hire top executives to run the firm on a day-to-day basis. The more stock a shareholder owns, the more votes that shareholder is entitled to cast for the company’s board of directors.
p43.zh: 当一家公司决定出售股票,哪些金融投资者可以买卖时,我们称之为公营公司.股东拥有一家上市公司. 由于股东群体非常广泛,往往由上千甚至上百万的投资者组成,股东们投票选举董事会,董事会又聘请高层高管来日常经营公司.股东拥有的股票越多,股东有权投给公司董事会的选票就越多.

p44.original: In theory, the board of directors helps to ensure that the firm runs in the interests of the true owners—the shareholders. However, the top executives who run the firm have a strong voice in choosing the candidates who will serve on their board of directors. After all, few shareholders are knowledgeable enough or have enough personal incentive to spend energy and money nominating alternative board members.
p44.zh: 从理论上讲,董事会有助于确保公司为真正的所有人——股东——的利益运作。 然而,管理事务所的高层高管在选择将任职于其董事会的候选人方面有着强烈的发言权.毕竟,很少有股东具备足够的知识或有足够的个人动机来花费精力和金钱来提名替代的董事会成员.

p45.original: How Firms Choose between Financial Capital Sources
p45.zh: 企业如何选择金融资本来源

p46.original: There are clear patterns in how businesses raise financial capital. We can explain these patterns in terms of imperfect information, which as we discussed in Information, Risk, and Insurance, is a situation where buyers and sellers in a market do not both have full and equal information. Those who are actually running a firm will almost always have more information about whether the firm is likely to earn profits in the future than outside investors who provide financial capital.
p46.zh: 企业筹集金融资本的方式有明显的规律. 我们可以用不完善的信息来解释这些模式,正如我们在《信息、风险和保险》中所讨论的那样,在一个市场上的买方和卖方都不具备充分和平等的信息。实际经营一家公司的人几乎总是比提供金融资本的外部投资者更了解该公司今后是否可能赚取利润。

p47.original: Any young startup firm is a risk. Some startup firms are only a little more than an idea on paper. The firm’s founders inevitably have better information than anyone else about how hard they are willing to work, and whether the firm is likely to succeed. When the founders invested their own money into the firm, they demonstrate a belief in its prospects. At this early stage, angel investors and venture capitalists try to overcome the imperfect information, at least in part, by knowing the managers and their business plan personally and by giving them advice.
p47.zh: 任何年轻的创业公司都是个风险。 一些创业公司只是纸上的想法而已.公司的创始人不可避免地比任何人都更了解他们愿意工作的难度,以及公司是否可能成功。 当创始人将自己的钱投入公司时,他们表现出了对公司前景的信念. 在这个早期阶段,天使投资者和风险资本家试图克服不完善的信息,至少部分地通过亲自了解管理者及其经营计划,并给他们建议.

p48.original: Accurate information is sometimes not available because corporate governance, the name economists give to the institutions that are supposed to watch over top executives, fails, as the following Clear It Up feature on Lehman Brothers shows.
p48.zh: 准确的信息有时无法提供,因为公司治理,即经济学家给那些应该监督高层管理人员的机构的称谓,失败了,正如雷曼兄弟的以下Clear It Up特征所显示的.

p49.original: How did lack of corporate governance lead to the Lehman Brothers failure?
p49.zh: 缺乏公司治理是如何导致雷曼兄弟破产的?

p50.original: In 2008, Lehman Brothers was the fourth largest U.S. investment bank, with 25,000 employees. The firm had been in business for 164 years. On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. There are many causes of the Lehman Brothers failure. One area of apparent failure was the lack of oversight by the Board of Directors to keep managers from undertaking excessive risk. We can attribute part of the oversight failure, according to Tim Geithner’s April 10, 2010, testimony to Congress, to the Executive Compensation Committee’s emphasis on short-term gains without enough consideration of the risks. In addition, according to the court examiner’s report, the Lehman Brother’s Board of Directors paid too little attention to the details of the operations of Lehman Brothers and also had limited financial service experience.
p50.zh: 2008年,雷曼兄弟是美国第四大投资银行,拥有25,000名员工.该公司已经营业164年。2008年9月15日,雷曼兄弟申请第11章破产保护.莱曼兄弟失败的原因很多.明显失败的一个领域是董事会缺乏监督,无法防止管理人员承担过度风险。 根据Tim Geithner2010年4月10日的言论, 我们可以将部分监督失败归咎于行政赔偿委员会强调短期收益, 而不充分考虑风险。 此外,根据法庭审查员的报告,雷曼兄弟的董事会对雷曼兄弟公司业务的细节关注太少,金融服务经验也有限.

p51.original: The board of directors, elected by the shareholders, is supposed to be the first line of corporate governance and oversight for top executives. A second institution of corporate governance is the auditing firm the company hires to review the company's financial records and certify that everything looks reasonable. A third institution of corporate governance is outside investors, especially large shareholders like those who invest large mutual funds or pension funds. In the case of Lehman Brothers, corporate governance failed to provide investors with accurate financial information about the firm’s operations.
p51.zh: 董事会由股东选举产生,应该是高层管理人员的公司治理和监督的第一线. 第二个公司治理机构是公司聘请的审计公司,以审查公司的财务记录,并证明一切看起来都是合理的。第三个公司治理机构是外部投资者,特别是投资大型共同基金或养恤基金的大股东。 就Lehman Brothers而言,公司治理未能向投资者提供关于公司业务的准确财务信息。

p52.original: As a firm becomes at least somewhat established and its strategy appears likely to lead to profits in the near future, knowing the individual managers and their business plans on a personal basis becomes less important, because information has become more widely available regarding the company’s products, revenues, costs, and profits. As a result, other outside investors who do not know the managers personally, like bondholders and shareholders, are more willing to provide financial capital to the firm.
p52.zh: 随着一家公司至少在一定程度上建立起来,而且其战略似乎在不久的将来有可能带来利润,了解个人管理人员及其个人商业计划就变得不那么重要,因为关于公司的产品、收入、成本和利润的信息已经更加广泛。 因此,其他不熟悉经理个人的外部投资者,如债券持有人和股东,更愿意为公司提供金融资本.

p53.original: At this point, a firm must often choose how to access financial capital. It may choose to borrow from a bank, issue bonds, or issue stock. The great disadvantage of borrowing money from a bank or issuing bonds is that the firm commits to scheduled interest payments, whether or not it has sufficient income. The great advantage of borrowing money is that the firm maintains control of its operations and is not subject to shareholders. Issuing stock involves selling off company ownership to the public and becoming responsible to a board of directors and the shareholders.
p53.zh: 此时,企业必须经常选择如何获得金融资本. 它可以选择向银行借款、发行债券或发行股票。向银行借钱或发行债券的最大缺点是,公司承诺按期支付利息,无论是否有足够的收入。借钱的一大优点是,公司保持对业务的控制,不受股东的支配.发行股票涉及向公众出售公司所有权,并对董事会和股东负责。

p54.original: The benefit of issuing stock is that a small and growing firm increases its visibility in the financial markets and can access large amounts of financial capital for expansion, without worrying about repaying this money. If the firm is successful and profitable, the board of directors will need to decide upon a dividend payout or how to reinvest profits to further grow the company. Issuing and placing stock is expensive, requires the expertise of investment bankers and attorneys, and entails compliance with reporting requirements to shareholders and government agencies, such as the federal Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
p54.zh: 发行股票的好处是,一家规模小且不断壮大的公司提高了其在金融市场的知名度,并可以获得大量金融资本用于扩张,而不必担心偿还这笔钱. 如果公司成功,盈利,董事会将需要决定股息的支付,或者如何再投资利润,以进一步壮大公司.股票发行和投放费用昂贵,需要投资银行家和律师的专业知识,并需要遵守股东和政府机构,如联邦证券交易委员会(证券交易委员会)的报告要求。

p56.original: Companies can raise early-stage financial capital in several ways: from their owners’ or managers’ personal savings, or credit cards and from private investors like angel investors and venture capital firms.
p56.zh: 公司可以通过几种方式筹集早期金融资本:从所有者或管理人员的个人储蓄或信用卡以及从天使投资者和风险资本公司等私人投资者那里筹集。

p57.original: A bond is a financial contract through which a borrower agrees to repay the amount that it borrowed. A bond specifies an amount that one will borrow, the amounts that one will repay over time based on the interest rate when the bond is issued, and the time until repayment. Corporate bonds are issued by firms; municipal bonds are issued by cities, state bonds by U.S. states, and Treasury bonds by the federal government through the U.S. Department of the Treasury.
p57.zh: 债券是指借款人同意偿还其借款金额的金融合同.保证书规定将借贷的金额,根据保证书发行时的利率,确定将偿还的金额,以及直至偿还的时间。公司债券由公司发行;市债券由城市发行,州债券由美国各州发行,国库债券由联邦政府通过美国发行.财政部.

p58.original: Stock represents firm ownership. A company's stock is divided into shares. A firm receives financial capital when it sells stock to the public. We call a company’s first stock sale to the public the initial public offering (IPO). However, a firm does not receive any funds when one shareholder sells stock in the firm to another investor. One receives the rate of return on stock in two forms: dividends and capital gains.
p58.zh: 股票代表公司所有权。公司股票分为股份.企业向公众出售股票时接受金融资本. 我们称公司首次向公众出售股票为首次公开出售(IPO)。 但是,当一股东将公司的股票出售给另一投资者时,公司不接收任何资金。一个人以两种形式获得股票收益率:股利和资本收益。

p59.original: A private company is usually owned by the people who run it on a day-to-day basis, although hired managers can run it. We call a private company owned and run by an individual a sole proprietorship, while a firm owned and run by a group is a partnership. When a firm decides to sell stock that financial investors can buy and sell, then the firm is owned by its shareholders—who in turn elect a board of directors to hire top day-to-day management. We call this a public company. Corporate governance is the name economists give to the institutions that are supposed to watch over top executives, though it does not always work.
p59.zh: 私人公司通常由日常经营的人拥有,虽然聘请的经理可以经营. 我们把个人拥有和经营的私营公司称为独资公司,而集团拥有和经营的公司则称为合伙公司。 当一家公司决定出售金融投资者可以买卖的股票时,该公司归其股东所有,股东又选出董事会聘请顶级的日常管理人员。 我们称这为公营公司。公司治理是经济学家给那些应该监督高层管理人员的机构取的名字,尽管它并不总是可行的。

p61.original:
Answer these three questions about early-stage corporate finance:
    
Why do very small companies tend to raise money from private investors instead of through an IPO?
Why do small, young companies often prefer an IPO to borrowing from a bank or issuing bonds?
Who has better information about whether a small firm is likely to earn profits, a venture capitalist or a potential bondholder, and why?
p61.zh: 回答关于早期公司融资的这三个问题:为什么非常小的公司倾向于向私人投资者募集资金,而不是通过IPO? 为什么年轻小公司往往更喜欢IPO而不是向银行借款或发行债券? 谁有更好的信息来说明一家小公司是否可能赚取利润、风险资本家或潜在债券持有人,以及为什么?

p62.original: The management of small companies might rather do an IPO right away, but until they get the company up and running, most people would not pay very much for the stock because of the risks involved.
p62.zh: 小公司的管理层可能宁可马上做IPO,但直到他们让公司上台和运行,大多数人不会因为涉及的风险而为股票支付很多费用.

p63.original: A small company may be earning few or zero profits, and its owners want to reinvest their earnings in the future growth of the company. If this company issues bonds or borrows money, it is obligated to make interest payments, which can eat up the company’s cash. If the company issues stock, it is not obligated to make payments to anyone (although it may choose to pay dividends).
p63.zh: 一个小公司可能利润很少或为零,其所有者希望将其收益再投资于公司未来的成长. 如果该公司发行债券或借钱,它有义务支付利息,利息可以消耗公司的现金。 如果公司发行股票,它没有义务向任何人付款(尽管它可能选择支付股息).

p64.original: Venture capitalists are private investors who can keep close tabs on the management and strategy of the company—and thus reduce the problems of imperfect information about whether the firm is being well run. Venture capitalists often own a substantial portion of the firm and have much better information than a typical shareholder would.
p64.zh: 风险资本家是私人投资者,他们可以密切监视公司的管理和战略,从而减少公司运作是否良好的不完善信息的问题。风险资本家往往拥有公司的大部分,拥有比典型股东更好的信息。

p65.original: From a firm’s point of view, how is a bond similar to a bank loan? How are they different?
p65.zh: 从公司的角度来看,债券如何类似于银行贷款? 他们有什么不同?

p66.original: From a firm’s point of view, a bond is very similar to a bank loan. Both are ways of borrowing money. Both require paying interest. The major difference is who must be persuaded to lend money: a bank loan requires persuading the bank, while issuing bonds requires persuading a number of separate bondholders. Since a bank often knows a great deal about a firm (especially if the firm has its accounts with that bank), bank loans are more common where imperfect information would otherwise be a problem.
p66.zh: 从公司的角度来看,债券与银行贷款非常相似。两者都是借钱的方式.两者都需要支付利息。主要的区别在于必须说服谁放贷:银行贷款需要说服银行,而发行债券则需要说服一些单独的债券持有人。 由于一家银行往往对一家公司了解甚多(特别是如果该公司在该银行有账户的话),银行贷款在不完善信息就会成为问题的地方更为常见。

p68.original: What are the most common ways for start-up firms to raise financial capital?
p68.zh: 创业企业筹集金融资本的最常见途径是什么?.

p69.original: Why can firms not just use their own profits for financial capital, with no need for outside investors?
p69.zh: 为什么企业不能仅仅将自己的利润用于金融资本,而不需要外部投资者呢?

p70.original: Why are banks more willing to lend to well-established firms?
p70.zh: 银行为什么更愿意向地位良好的公司贷款?

p72.original: What does a share of stock represent?

p73.original: When do firms receive money from a stock sale in their firm and when do they not receive money?
p73.zh: 公司何时从公司股票销售中收到资金,何时不收到资金?

p76.original: What is the difference between a private company and a public company?
p76.zh: 民营公司与公营公司有何区别?.

p77.original: How do the shareholders who own a company choose the actual company managers?
p77.zh: 拥有公司的股东如何选择实际公司经理?

p79.original: If you owned a small firm that had become somewhat established, but you needed a surge of financial capital to carry out a major expansion, would you prefer to raise the funds through borrowing or by issuing stock? Explain your choice.
p79.zh: 如果你拥有一家小公司, 已经有些建立起来, 但你需要大量金融资本来进行大规模扩张, 你会愿意通过借贷或发行股票来筹集资金吗?解释你的选择。

p80.original: Explain how a company can fail when the safeguards that should be in place fail.
p80.zh: 解释当应实施的保障措施失败时,公司如何会失败.

p82.original: The Darkroom Windowshade Company has 100,000 shares of stock outstanding. The investors in the firm own the following numbers of shares: investor 1 has 20,000 shares; investor 2 has 18,000 shares; investor 3 has 15,000 shares; investor 4 has 10,000 shares; investor 5 has 7,000 shares; and investors 6 through 11 have 5,000 shares each. What is the minimum number of investors it would take to vote to change the company's top management? If investors 1 and 2 agree to vote together, can they be certain of always getting their way in how the company will be run?
p82.zh: 暗室窗荫公司有10万股股股权未清.公司投资者拥有的股份数量如下:投资者1有2万股;投资者2有1万8千股;投资者3有1万5千股;投资者4有1万股;投资者5有7000股;投资者6至11有5千股.改变公司最高管理层的投票最低投资者人数是多少?. 如果投资人1号和2号同意一起投票,他们能否肯定总是能掌握公司的运作方式?

p87.zh: 家庭如何提供金融资本

p88.original: The ways in which firms would prefer to raise funds are only half the story of financial markets. The other half is what those households and individuals who supply funds desire, and how they perceive the available choices. The focus of our discussion now shifts from firms on the demand side of financial capital markets to households on the supply side of those markets. We can divide the mechanisms for savings available to households into several categories: deposits in bank accounts; bonds; stocks; money market mutual funds; stock and bond mutual funds; and housing and other tangible assets like owning gold. We need to analyze each of these investments in terms of three factors: (1) the expected rate of return it will pay; (2) the risk that the return will be much lower or higher than expected; and (3) the investment's liquidity, which refers to how easily one can exchange money or financial assets for a good or service. We will do this analysis as we discuss each of these investments in the sections below. First, however, we need to understand the difference between expected rate of return, risk, and actual rate of return.
p88.zh: 公司倾向于筹集资金的方式只是金融市场的一半。另一半是那些提供资金的家庭和个人所希望的,以及他们对现有选择的看法。 我们的讨论重点现在从金融资本市场需求方的公司转向这些市场供应方的家庭。 我们可以将家庭储蓄机制分为几类:银行账户存款、债券、股票、货币市场共同基金、股票和债券共同基金以及住房和其他有形资产,如拥有黄金。 我们需要从三个因素来分析这些投资的每一项:(1) 其预期收益率;(2) 收益比预期低得多或高得多的风险;(3) 投资的流动性,指人们如何容易地将金钱或金融资产换成货物或服务。 我们将在下文各节讨论这些投资时进行这一分析。 但是,首先,我们需要了解预期回报率、风险和实际回报率之间的差别。

p89.original: Expected Rate of Return, Risk, and Actual Rate of Return
p89.zh: 预期回返率、风险和实际回返率

p90.original: The expected rate of return refers to how much a project or an investment is expected to return to the investor, either in future interest payments, capital gains, or increased profitability. It is usually the average return over a period of time, usually in years or even decades. We normally measure it as a percentage rate. Risk measures the uncertainty of that project’s profitability. There are several types of risk, including default risk and interest rate risk. Default risk, as its name suggests, is the risk that the borrower fails to pay back the bond or loan. Interest rate risk is the danger that you might buy a long term bond at a 6% interest rate right before market rates suddenly rise, so had you waited, you could have received a similar bond that paid 9%. A high-risk investment is one for which a wide range of potential payoffs is reasonably probable. A low-risk investment may have actual returns that are fairly close to its expected rate of return year after year. A high-risk investment will have actual returns that are much higher than the expected rate of return in some months or years and much lower in other months or years. The actual rate of return refers to the total rate of return, including capital gains and interest paid on an investment at the end of a time period.
p90.zh: 预期收益率是指项目或投资预期能向投资者回报多少,无论是未来利息支付、资本收益还是增加利润。通常是一段时间内的平均回报率,通常在几年甚至几十年内. 我们通常以百分率衡量。风险衡量该项目利润的不确定性。 有几种风险,包括违约风险和利率风险。 如其名称所示,默认风险是借款人未能还清债券或贷款的风险。利率风险是指你可能在市场利率突然上升之前以6%的利率购买长期债券的风险,所以如果你等待,你本可以收到一个支付9%的类似债券.高风险投资是有可能获得广泛潜在回报的投资。低风险投资的实际回报率可能相当接近年复一年的预期回报率。高风险投资的实际回报率在一些月或几年中将远远高于预期回报率,在其他几个月或几年中则低得多。实际收益率是指总收益率,包括资本收益和某一时期终了时投资支付的利息.

p92.original: An intermediary is one who stands between two other parties. For example, a person who arranges a blind date between two other people is one kind of intermediary. In financial capital markets, banks are an example of a financial intermediary—that is, an institution that operates between a saver who deposits funds in a bank and a borrower who receives a loan from that bank. When a bank serves as a financial intermediary, unlike the situation with a couple on a blind date, the saver and the borrower never meet. In fact, it is not even possible to make direct connections between those who deposit funds in banks and those who borrow from banks, because all deposited funds end up in one big pool, which the financial institution then lends out.
p92.zh: 中间人是站在其他两个当事方中间的人。 例如,安排另外两个人之间的相亲是一类中介. 在金融资本市场上,银行是金融中介机构的一个范例,即储蓄者在银行存款和接受银行贷款的借款人之间开展业务的机构。 当一家银行作为金融中介时,不同于一对夫妇在相亲时的情况,储蓄者和借款者从不见面. 事实上,在银行存款的人和向银行借款的人之间甚至不可能建立直接联系,因为所有存入的资金都最后都集中在一个大池中,然后由金融机构借出。

p93.original: illustrates the position of banks as a financial intermediary, with a pattern of deposits flowing into a bank and loans flowing out, and then repayment of the loans flowing back to the bank, with interest payments for the original savers.
p93.zh: 说明银行作为金融中介的地位,银行的存款和贷款都流入银行,然后还本付息,然后还本付息。

p94.zh: 银行作为金融中介机构

p95.original: Banks offer a range of accounts to serve different needs. A checking account typically pays little or no interest, but it facilitates transactions by giving you easy access to your money, either by writing a check or by using a debit card (that is, a card which works like a credit card, except that purchases are immediately deducted from your checking account rather than billed separately through a credit card company). A savings account typically pays some interest rate, but getting the money typically requires you to make a trip to the bank or an automatic teller machine (or you can access the funds electronically). The lines between checking and savings accounts have blurred in the last couple of decades, as many banks offer checking accounts that will pay an interest rate similar to a savings account if you keep a certain minimum amount in the account, or conversely, offer savings accounts that allow you to write at least a few checks per month.
p95.zh: 银行提供一系列账户以满足不同的需要。支票账户通常支付很少或没有利息,但通过方便您获取资金,通过写支票或使用借记卡(即像信用卡一样起作用的卡,但购买立即从您的支票账户中扣除,而不是通过信用卡公司单独开出账单)来方便交易.储蓄账户通常支付一定的利率,但获得资金通常需要你去银行旅行或自动出纳机(或者你可以以电子方式获取资金). 过去几十年中,支票账户和储蓄账户之间的界限模糊不清,因为许多银行都提供支票账户,如果在账户中保留一定的最低金额,那么这些账户将支付类似于储蓄账户的利率,或者反之,提供储蓄账户,允许你每月至少写几张支票。

p96.original: Another way to deposit savings at a bank is to use a certificate of deposit (CD). With a CD, you agree to deposit a certain amount of money, often measured in thousands of dollars, in the account for a stated period of time, typically ranging from a few months to several years. In exchange, the bank agrees to pay a higher interest rate than for a regular savings account. While you can withdraw the money before the allotted time, as the advertisements for CDs always warn, there is “a substantial penalty for early withdrawal.”
p96.zh: 将存款存入银行的另一种方法是使用存款证明(CD).有了一张CD,你同意将一定数额的钱存入帐户,通常以几千美元计,规定一段时间,一般从几个月到几年不等. 作为交换,银行同意支付高于经常储蓄账户的利率.CD的广告总是警告您可以在分配的时间之前收回这笔钱,

p97.original: shows the annual rate of interest paid on a six-month, one-year, and five-year CD since 1984, as reported by Bankrate.com. The interest rates that savings accounts pay are typically a little lower than the CD rate, because financial investors need to receive a slightly higher rate of interest as compensation for promising to leave deposits untouched for a period of time in a CD, and thus forfeiting some liquidity.
p97.zh: 显示Bankrate.com报告的1984年以来6个月、1年和5年CD的年利率。储蓄账户支付的利率通常略低于CD利率,因为金融投资者需要获得略高的利率,作为对承诺在CD中保留一段时间不受影响存款的补偿,从而失去一些流动性。

p98.original: Interest Rates on Six-Month, One-Year, and Five-Year Certificates of Deposit
p98.zh: 6个月、1年和5年存款证明的利率

p99.original: The great advantages of bank accounts are that financial investors have very easy access to their money, and also money in bank accounts is extremely safe. In part, this safety arises because a bank account offers more security than keeping a few thousand dollars in the toe of a sock in your underwear drawer. In addition, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) protects the savings of the average person. Every bank is required by law to pay a fee to the FDIC, based on the size of its deposits. Then, if a bank should go bankrupt and not be able to repay depositors, the FDIC guarantees that all customers will receive their deposits back up to $250,000.
p99.zh: 银行账户的巨大优点是金融投资者能够非常容易地获得他们的钱,银行账户中的钱也是极其安全的.部分地说,这种安全性 是因为银行帐户比在你的内裤抽屉里 留着一只袜子的脚趾 提供了更多的安全性。 此外,联邦存款保险公司保护普通人的储蓄。法律规定,每个银行都必须根据其存款规模向外国资本管制中心支付费用。 然后,如果一家银行破产,无法偿还存款人,FDIC保证所有客户都能收到高达25万美元的存款。

p100.original: The bottom line on bank accounts looks like this: low risk means low rate of return but high liquidity.
p100.zh: 银行账户的底线是这样的:低风险意味着回报率低但流动性高.

p102.original: An investor who buys a bond expects to receive a rate of return. However, bonds vary in the rates of return that they offer, according to the riskiness of the borrower. We always can divide an interest rate into three components (as we explained in Choice in a World of Scarcity): compensation for delaying consumption, an adjustment for an inflationary rise in the overall level of prices, and a risk premium that takes the borrower’s riskiness into account.
p102.zh: 购买债券的投资者预期会得到收益率。 然而,债券的回报率因借款人的风险而异。 我们总是可以将利率分为三个部分(正如我们在《世界危机的选择》中解释的 ) : 对拖延消费的补偿、对通货膨胀上升的总体价格水平的调整以及考虑到借款人风险的风险溢价。

p103.original: The U.S. government is an extremely safe borrower, so when the U.S. government issues Treasury bonds, it can pay a relatively low interest rate. Firms that appear to be safe borrowers, perhaps because of their sheer size or because they have consistently earned profits over time, will pay a higher interest rate than the U.S. government. Firms that appear to be riskier borrowers, perhaps because they are still growing or their businesses appear shaky, will pay the highest interest rates when they issue bonds. We call bonds that offer high interest rates to compensate for their relatively high chance of default high-yield bonds or junk bonds. A number of today’s well-known firms issued junk bonds in the 1980s when they were starting to grow, including Turner Broadcasting and Microsoft.
p103.zh: 美国政府是极安全的借款人,因此当美国政府发行国库债券时,可以支付相对较低的利率.似乎安全借款的公司,或许是因为它们规模庞大,或因为它们在一段时间内不断赚取利润,将支付比美国政府更高的利率。似乎较有风险的借款人,也许由于他们仍在成长或生意似乎摇摇欲坠,在发行债券时将支付最高的利率。 我们要求提供高利率的债券来补偿其较高的违约高收益债券或废品债券的可能性。 今天的一些知名公司在1980年代开始成长时发行了垃圾债券,包括特纳广播和微软.

p104.original: Visit this website to read about Treasury bonds.
p104.zh: 访问此网站阅读国库债券.

p105.original: A bond issued by the U.S. government or a large corporation may seem to be relatively low risk: after all, the bond issuer has promised to make certain payments over time, and except for rare bankruptcy cases, these payments will occur. If a corporate bond issuer fails to make the payments that it owes to its bondholders, the bondholders can require that the company declare bankruptcy, sell off its assets, and pay them as much as it can. Even in the case of junk bonds, a wise investor can reduce the risk by purchasing bonds from a wide range of different companies since, even if a few firms go broke and do not pay, they are not all likely to go bankrupt.
p105.zh: 美国政府或大公司发行的债券,其风险可能似乎相对较低:毕竟,债券发行人已经承诺会随着时间推移进行一定的支付,除罕见的破产案件外,这些支付都会发生.公司债券发行人未按规定向债券持有人支付所欠款项的,债券持有人可以要求公司申报破产,变卖其资产,并尽量支付.即使是垃圾债券,明智的投资者也可以通过从各种不同的公司购买债券来降低风险,因为即使少数公司破产而不付款,它们也不可能全部破产。

p106.original:
As we noted before, bonds carry an interest rate risk. For example, imagine you decide to buy a 10-year bond for $1,000 that would pay an annual interest rate of 8%. Soon after you buy the bond, interest rates on bonds rise, so that now similar companies are paying an annual rate of 12%. Anyone who buys a $1,000 bond now can receive annual payments of $120 per year, but since your bond was issued at an interest rate of 8%, you have tied up $1,000 and receive payments of only $80 per year. In the meaningful sense of opportunity cost, you are missing out on the higher payments that you could have received. Furthermore, you can calculate the amount you should be willing to pay now for future payments. To place a present discounted value on a future payment, decide what you would need in the present to equal a certain amount in the
  future. This calculation will require an interest rate. For example, if the interest rate is 25%, then a payment of $125 a year from now will have a present discounted value of $100—that is, you could take $100 in the present and have $125 in the future. (We discuss this further in the appendix on Present Discounted Value.)
p106.zh: 正如我们以前指出的,债券带有利率风险。 例如,想象一下,你决定以1000美元购买10年的债券,以支付8%的年利率。 在购买债券后不久,债券利率就上升了,因此现在类似的公司每年支付12%的利率。 现在买1000元债券的任何人都可以每年得到120元的年付款,但是由于你的债券是以8%的利率发行的,所以你已经捆绑了1000元,每年只得到80元的付款. 从机会成本的有意义的意义上讲,你忽略了本可以得到的更高金额的付款。 此外,您还可以计算您现在愿意支付的未来支付金额。将现值折现值投放未来付款时,决定您目前需要的金额,以在未来达到一定金额. 这种计算需要利率。 例如,如果利率是25%,那么从现在起每年125美元的付款将有一个100美元的现值折扣,也就是说,你现在可以拿100美元,将来可以拿125美元。(我们在关于目前折扣价值的附录中进一步讨论了这一点。 )

p107.original: In financial terms, a bond has several parts. A bond is basically an “I owe you” note that an investor receives in exchange for capital (money). The bond has a face value. This is the amount the borrower agrees to pay the investor at maturity. The bond has a coupon rate or interest rate, which is usually semi-annual, but can be paid at different times throughout the year. (Bonds used to be paper documents with coupons that investors clipped and turned in to the bank to receive interest.) The bond has a maturity date when the borrower will pay back its face value as well as its last interest payment. Combining the bond’s face value, interest rate, and maturity date, and market interest rates, allows a buyer to compute a bond’s present value, which is the most that a buyer would be willing to pay for a given bond. This may or may not be the same as the face value.
p107.zh: 在财务方面,债券有几个部分。债券基本上是投资者收到的“我欠你的”票据,以换取资本(金钱)。债券有面值. 这是借款人在到期时同意向投资者支付的数额。债券有券利率或利率,利率通常为半年,但全年可以在不同时间支付.(这些债券以前是纸质文件,有投资者剪辑的券,然后交给银行收取利息。 )债券有一个到期日,借款人将偿还其面值以及最后的利息付款。将债券的面值、利率和到期日以及市场利率结合起来,就可以使买方计算债券的现值,这是买方最愿意支付特定债券的。这可能与面值相同,也可能不同.

p108.original: The bond yield measures the rate of return a bond is expected to pay over time. Investors can buy bonds when they are issued and they can buy and sell them during their lifetimes. When buying a bond that has been around for a few years, investors should know that the interest rate printed on a bond is often not the same as the bond yield, even on new bonds. Read the next Work It Out feature to see how this happens.
p108.zh: 保证金收益量是保证金预期随时间推移而支付的回报率。投资者在债券发行时可以购买债券,在存续期间可以买卖债券.投资者在购买已经存在几年的债券时,应当知道债券上印出的利率往往与债券收益不相同,即使是对新债券也不相同.读下一首《工作》的功能,看看会怎样发生。

p110.original: You have bought a $1,000 bond whose coupon rate is 8%. To calculate your return or yield, follow these steps:
p110.zh: 你买了1000元的债券 其优惠券利率是8% 为计算返回或收益率,请遵循这些步骤:

p111.original:
Assume the following:
  Face value of a bond: $1,000Coupon rate: 8 %
  Annual payment: $80 per year
p111.zh: 假定: 债券的面值:1 000美元

p112.original: Consider the risk of the bond. If this bond carries no risk, then it would be safe to assume that the bond will sell for $1,000 when it is issued and pay the purchaser $80 per year until its maturity, at which time the final interest payment will be made and the original $1,000 will be repaid. Now, assume that over time the interest rates prevailing in the economy rise to 12% and that there is now only one year left to this bond’s maturity. This makes the bond an unattractive investment, since an investor can find another bond that perhaps pays 12%. To induce the investor to buy the 8% bond, the bond seller will lower its price below its face value of $1,000.
p112.zh: 考虑保证金的风险. 如果这种保证书没有风险,那么可以假定,保证书在发行时会以1000美元出售,并每年向购买者支付80美元直至到期,届时将支付最后利息,并偿还原1000美元。 现在,假设随着时间的推移,经济中普遍存在的利率上升到12%,而现在这一债券的到期只剩下一年的时间了。这使得债券成为无吸引力的投资,因为投资者可以找到另一种可能支付12%的债券。 为了诱导投资者购买8%的债券,债券销售者将把其价格降低到低于面值1000美元的水平.

p113.original: Calculate the bond's price when its interest rate is less than the market interest rate. The expected payments from the bond one year from now are $1,080, because in the bond’s last year the bond's issuer will make the final interest payment and then also repay the original $1,000. Given that interest rates are now 12%, you know that you could invest $964 in an alternative investment and receive $1,080 a year from now; that is, $964(1 + 0.12) = $1080. Therefore, you will not pay more than $964 for the original $1,000 bond.
p113.zh: 债券利率低于市场利率时计算债券价格.债券的预期付款是1 080美元,因为在债券的最后一年,债券的发行人将支付最后利息,然后还原1 000美元。 鉴于现在利率为12%,你知道你可以投资964美元作为替代投资,并且从现在起每年获得1 080美元,即964(1+0.12)=1080美元。 因此,您不会支付超过964美元的原始1000美元保证金.

p114.original: Consider that the investor will receive the $1,000 face value, plus $80 for the last year’s interest payment. The yield on the bond will be ($1080 – $964)/$964 = 12%. The yield, or total return, means interest payments, plus capital gains. Note that the interest or coupon rate of 8% did not change. When interest rates rise, bonds previously issued at lower interest rates will sell for less than face value. Conversely, when interest rates fall, bonds previously issued at higher interest rates will sell for more than face value.
p114.zh: 考虑投资方将获得1 000美元的面值,加上去年支付利息的80美元。债券的收益将为(1080美元-964美元/964美元=12%)。收益率,或总收益,是指支付利息,加上资本收益.请注意,8%的利率或优惠券利率没有变化。 当利率上升时,先前发行的利率较低的债券将以低于面值的价格出售.反之,当利率下降时,以前以较高利率发行的债券的售价将超过面值。

p115.original: shows bond yield for two kinds of bonds: 10-year Treasury bonds (which are officially called “notes”) and corporate bonds issued by firms that have been given an AAA rating as relatively safe borrowers by Moody’s, an independent firm that publishes such ratings. Even though corporate bonds pay a higher interest rate, because firms are riskier borrowers than the federal government, the rates tend to rise and fall together. Treasury bonds typically pay more than bank accounts, and corporate bonds typically pay a higher interest rate than Treasury bonds.
p115.zh: 显示两种债券的债券收益率:10年期国库债券(正式称为 " 钞票 " )和公司发行的公司债券,这些公司被穆迪公司(一家公布这种评级的独立公司)评为相对安全的借款人。 即使公司债券支付较高的利率,因为公司比联邦政府更具有风险的借款人,但利率往往同时上升和下降.国库债券一般支付比银行账户多,公司债券通常支付比国库债券更高的利率.

p116.original: Interest Rates for Corporate Bonds and Ten-Year U.S. Treasury Bonds
p116.zh: 公司债券利率与十年美国利率.国库债券

p117.original: The bottom line for bonds: rate of return—low to moderate, depending on the borrower's risk; risk—low to moderate, depending on whether interest rates in the economy change substantially after the bond is issued; liquidity—moderate, because the investor needs to sell the bond before the investor regains the cash.
p117.zh: 债券的底线:收益率——根据借款人的风险而从低到中;风险——从低到中,取决于债券发行后经济利率是否发生重大变化;流动性——中度,因为投资者需要在投资者收回现金之前出售债券。

p119.original: As we stated earlier, the rate of return on a financial investment in a share of stock can come in two forms: as dividends paid by the firm and as a capital gain achieved by selling the stock for more than you paid. The range of possible returns from buying stock is mind-bending. Firms can decide to pay dividends or not. A stock price can rise to a multiple of its original price or sink all the way to zero. Even in short periods of time, well-established companies can see large movements in their stock prices. For example, on July 1, 2011, Netflix stock peaked at $295 per share; one year later, on July 30, 2012, it was at $53.91 per share; in 2022, it had recovered to $199. When Facebook went public, its shares of stock sold for around $40 per share, but in 2022, they were selling for slightly over $212.
p119.zh: 正如我们早些时候指出的,股票份额的金融投资回报率可以有两种形式:作为公司支付的股利,作为出售股票所得的资本收益,所得金额超过你支付的数额。购买股票可能带来的收益范围是心智的延伸。公司可以决定支付股息与否.股价可以升至其原价的倍数,也可以一直下沉到零.即使在短时期内,地位良好的公司也能看到其股票价格的大幅波动. 例如,2011年7月1日,Netflix股票达到顶峰,每股295美元;一年后,2012年7月30日,每股53.91美元;2022年,已恢复到199美元. 当Facebook公开时,其股票股票的售价为每股40美元左右,但在2022年时,其售价略高于212美元.

p120.original: We will discuss the reasons why stock prices fall and rise so abruptly below, but first you need to know how we measure stock market performance. There are a number of different ways to measure the overall performance of the stock market, based on averaging different subsets of companies' stock prices. Perhaps the best-known stock market measure is the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which is based on 30 large U.S. companies' stock prices. Another stock market performance gauge, the Standard & Poor’s 500, follows the stock prices of the 500 largest U.S. companies. The Wilshire 5000 tracks the stock prices of essentially all U.S. companies that have stock the public can buy and sell.
p120.zh: 我们将讨论股价跌落和暴涨的原因 但首先你需要知道我们如何衡量股票市场业绩。 根据公司股票价格的不同子集的平均值,衡量股票市场的整体业绩有几种不同的方法. 也许最知名的股市衡量标准是道琼斯工业平均指数,该指数基于美国30家大公司的股价.另一股市场表现表,标准普尔500股,跟随美国500大公司的股价.威尔希尔5000号追踪了几乎所有拥有公众股票的美国公司的股票价格,这些公司可以买卖.

p121.original: Other stock market measures focus on where stocks are traded. For example, the New York Stock Exchange monitors the performance of stocks that are traded on that exchange in New York City. The Nasdaq stock market includes about 3,600 stocks, with a concentration of technology stocks.  lists some of the most commonly cited measures of U.S. and international stock markets.
p121.zh: 其他股票市场措施的重点是股票交易地点。 例如,纽约证券交易所监测在纽约市该交易所交易的股票的业绩。纳斯达克股票市场包括约3600种股票,技术股票集中. 納斯達克股票市场列出美国和国际股票市场最常引用的一些措施.

p126.original: Based on 30 large companies from a diverse set of representative industries, chosen by analysts at Dow Jones and Company. The index was started in 1896.
p126.zh: 以30家大型公司为基础,这些公司来自多种代表性行业,由道琼斯和公司的分析师选择. 该指数始于1896年.

p127.zh: 标准普尔的500:http://www.standpoors.com 标准普尔公司(英语:Standardandpoors.

p128.original: Based on 500 large U.S. firms, chosen by analysts at Standard & Poor’s to represent the economy as a whole.
p128.zh: 由标准普尔公司的分析师选择,

p130.original: Includes essentially all U.S. companies with stock ownership. Despite the name, this index includes about 7,000 firms.
p130.zh: 基本上包括所有拥有股票所有权的美国公司。 尽管有这个名字,这个指数包括大约7000家公司.

p132.original: The oldest and largest U.S. stock market, dating back to 1792. It trades stocks for 2,800 companies of all sizes. It is located at 18 Broad St. in New York City.
p132.zh: 美国最古老和最大的股票市场,可以追溯到1792年. 它为2 800家各种规模的公司进行股票交易。 它位于纽约市的Broad St. 18号.

p134.original: Founded in 1971 as an electronic stock market, allowing people to buy or sell from many physical locations. It has about 3,600 companies.
p134.zh: 成立于1971年,是一个电子股票市场,允许人们从许多实体地点进行买卖. 它拥有约3600家公司.

p136.original: Includes the 100 largest companies on the London Stock Exchange. Pronounced “footsie.” Originally stood for Financial Times Stock Exchange.
p136.zh: 包括伦敦证券交易所的100家最大公司.发音是“footsie ” 。 最初是金融时报证券交易所的会员。

p138.original: Nikkei stands for Nihon Keizai Shimbun, which translates as the Japan Economic Journal, a major business newspaper in Japan. Index includes the 225 largest and most actively traded stocks on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
p138.zh: Nikkei代表日本主要商业报纸日本经济报(日语:日本經濟報)译作"日本经济报"(日语:日本经济报).指数包括东京证券交易所225家最大且交易最活跃的股票.

p140.original: Tracks 30 of the largest companies on the Frankfurt, Germany, stock exchange. DAX is an abbreviation for Deutscher Aktien Index (German Stock Index).
p140.zh: 德国法兰克福最大的30家公司的轨迹,证券交易所.DAX是德意志国阿克蒂安指数(德语:Deutscher Aktien Index)的缩写.

p141.original: The trend in the stock market is generally up over time, but with some large dips along the way.  shows the path of the Standard & Poor’s 500 index (which is measured on the left-hand vertical axis) and the Dow Jones Index (which is measured on the right-hand vertical axis). Broad stock market measures, like the ones we list here, tend to move together. The S&P 500 Index is the weighted average market capitalization of the firms selected to be in the index. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is the price weighted average of 30 industrial stocks tracked on the New York Stock Exchange.
p141.zh: 股市趋势一般随时间推移而上升,但沿途有一些大的倾斜. 显示了标准普尔500指数(由左侧垂直轴测量)和道琼斯指数(由右侧垂直轴测量)的路径.广泛的股票市场措施,就像我们在这里列出的,往往会一起移动。S&P 500指数是被选入指数的公司加权平均市场资本化.道琼斯工业平均值是纽约证券交易所追踪到的30种工业股票的价格加权平均值.

p142.original: When the Dow Jones average rises from 5,000 to 10,000, you know that the average price of the stocks in that index has roughly doubled.  shows that stock prices did not rise much in the 1970s, but then started a steady climb in the 1980s. From 2000 to 2013, stock prices bounced up and down, but ended up at about the same level.
p142.zh: 当道琼斯的平均价格从5000美元上升到10,000美元时,你知道该指数中股票的平均价格大约翻了一番. 这表明股票价格在1970年代没有多大上涨,但随后在1980年代开始稳步攀升. 从2000年到2013年,股价上下回弹,但最终仍维持了约同一水平.

p143.original: The Dow Jones Industrial Index and the Standard & Poor’s 500, 1965–2021
p143.zh: Dow Jones工业指数和标准普尔500指数,1965-2021

p144.original: shows the total annual rate of return an investor would have received from buying the stocks in the S&P 500 index over recent decades. The total return here includes both dividends paid by these companies and also capital gains arising from increases in the stock value. (For technical reasons related to how we calculate the numbers, the dividends and capital gains do not add exactly to the total return.) From the 1950s to the 1980s, the average firm paid annual dividends equal to about 4% of its stock value. Since the 1990s, dividends have dropped and now often provide a return closer to 1% to 2%. In the 1960s and 1970s, the gap between percent earned on capital gains and dividends was much closer than it has been since the 1980s. In the 1980s and 1990s, capital gains were far higher than dividends. In the 2000s, dividends remained low and, while stock prices fluctuated, they ended the decade roughly where they had started. In the 2010s, dividends remained low and stock prices increased, and this continued at the beginning of the 2020s.
p144.zh: 显示投资者在最近几十年购买S&P 500指数股票时会得到的总年收益率。 这里的总收益包括这些公司支付的股利和股票价值增加所产生的资本收益。(与我们如何计算数字有关的技术原因,股息和资本收益并不确切地增加总收益. ) 从20世纪50年代到80年代,平均公司支付的年股息相当于其股价的4%左右. 自1990年代以来,股息下降,现在往往提供接近1%至2%的回报。 在1960年代和1970年代,从资本收益和股息中挣得的百分比差距比1980年代以来要近得多。 在1980年代和1990年代,资本收益远高于股息。 在2000年代,股息仍然很低,虽然股票价格波动,但股息大致结束了开始的十年。2010年代,股息仍然很低,股价上升,这在2020年代初仍在继续.

p186.original: The overall pattern is that stocks as a group have provided a high rate of return over extended periods of time, but this return comes with risks. The market value of individual companies can rise and fall substantially, both over short time periods and over the long run. During extended periods of time like the 1970s or the first decade of the 2000s, the overall stock market return can be quite modest. The stock market can sometimes fall sharply, as it did in 2008.
p186.zh: 总体模式是,库存作为一个群体在很长一段时间内提供了很高的回报率,但这种回报带来风险。单个公司的市场价值无论在短期还是长期内都可能大幅上升和下降。 在20世纪70年代或2000年代头十年等长时间内,总的股市回报率可以相当低.股市有时会像2008年那样急剧下跌.

p187.original: The bottom line on investing in stocks is that the rate of return over time will be high, but the risks are also high, especially in the short run. Liquidity is also high since one can sell stock in publicly held companies readily for spendable money.
p187.zh: 关于股票投资的底线是,一段时间内收益率会很高,但风险也很高,特别是短期内。流动性也很高,因为人们可以随时出售公有公司的股票,以换取可花的钱。

p189.original: Buying stocks or bonds issued by a single company is always somewhat risky. An individual firm may find itself buffeted by unfavorable supply and demand conditions or hurt by unlucky or unwise managerial decisions. Thus, a standard recommendation from financial investors is diversification, which means buying stocks or bonds from a wide range of companies. A saver who diversifies is following the old proverb: “Don’t put all your eggs in one basket.” In any broad group of companies, some firms will do better than expected and some will do worse—but the diversification has a tendency to cancel out extreme increases and decreases in value.
p189.zh: 购买单个公司发行的股票或债券总是有些风险。个别公司可能发现自己受到不合适的供求条件的冲击,或受到不吉利或不明智的管理决定的伤害。 因此,金融投资者的标准建议是多样化,这意味着从各种公司购买股票或债券。 一个多样化的储蓄者遵循了古老的谚语 : “ 不要把你所有的鸡蛋都放在一个篮子里。 ”在任何广泛的公司集团中,有些公司会做得比预期的好,有些公司会做得更差 — — 但多样化往往会抵消价值的极端增减。

p190.original: Purchasing a diversified group of stocks or bonds has become easier in the internet age, but it remains something of a task. To simplify the process, companies offer mutual funds, which consist of a variety of stocks or bonds from different companies. The financial investor buys mutual fund shares, and then receives a return based on how the fund as a whole performs. In 2021, according to the Investment Company Factbook, just over 47% of U.S. households had a financial investment in a mutual fund—including many people who have their retirement savings or pension money invested in this way.
p190.zh: 购买多样化的股票或债券在互联网时代已经变得容易了,但这仍然是一项任务。 为了简化程序,公司提供共同基金,由不同公司的各种股票或债券组成。金融投资人购买共同基金股份,然后根据基金整体运作情况获得收益.2021年,根据投资公司"事实手册",只有47%以上的美国家庭对共同基金有财务投资——包括许多以这种方式投资其退休储蓄或养老金的人.

p191.original: Mutual funds can focus in certain areas: one mutual fund might invest only in company stocks based in Indonesia, or only in bonds issued by large manufacturing companies, or only in biotechnology companies' stock. At the other end of the spectrum, a mutual fund might be quite broad. At the extreme, some mutual funds own a tiny share of every firm in the stock market, and thus the mutual fund's value will fluctuate with the overall stock market's average. We call a mutual fund that seeks only to mimic the market's overall performance an index fund.
p191.zh: 共同基金可以集中于某些领域:一个共同基金可能只投资于设在印度尼西亚的公司股票,或只投资于大型制造公司发行的债券,或只投资于生物技术公司的股票。 另一方面,共同基金可能相当广泛。极端情况下,一些共同基金在股票市场上拥有每家公司的极小份额,因此共同基金的价值会随整个股票市场的平均值而波动. 我们称一个共同基金只是模仿市场的整体业绩,而是一种指数基金。

p192.original: Diversification can offset some of the risks of individual stocks rising or falling. Even investors who buy an indexed mutual fund designed to mimic some measure of the broad stock market, like the Standard & Poor’s 500, had better prepare against some ups and downs, like those the stock market experienced in the first decade of the 2000s. In 2008 average U.S. stock funds declined 38%, reducing individual and household wealth. This steep drop in value hit hardest those who were close to retirement and were counting on their stock funds to supplement retirement income.
p192.zh: 多样化可以抵消个别股票上升或下降的一些风险。即使是那些购买指数化的共同基金,旨在模仿大股市某种度量的投资者,如标准普尔(Standard & Poor)的500强,也比2000年代头十年股市所经历的一些起伏更能做好准备。2008年,美国平均股票基金下降了38%,减少了个人和家庭财富。 这种价值的急剧下降对那些接近退休并依靠其股票资金来补充退休收入的人打击最大。

p193.original: The bottom line on investing in mutual funds is that the rate of return over time will be high. The risks are also high, but the risks and returns for an individual mutual fund will be lower than those for an individual stock. As with stocks, liquidity is also high provided the mutual fund or stock index fund is readily traded.
p193.zh: 共同基金投资的底线是,随着时间的推移,收益率将很高。风险也很高,但个人共同基金的风险和收益将低于个人股票的风险和收益。与股票一样,如果共同基金或股票指数基金易于交易,流动性也很高。

p195.original: Households can also seek a rate of return by purchasing tangible assets, especially housing. About two-thirds of U.S. households own their own home. An owner’s equity in a house is the monetary value the owner would have after selling the house and repaying any outstanding bank loans they used to buy the house. For example, imagine that you buy a house for $200,000, paying 10% of the price as a down payment and taking out a bank loan for the remaining $180,000. Over time, you pay off some of your bank loan, so that only $100,000 remains, and the house's value on the market rises to $250,000. At that point, your equity in the home is the value of the home minus the value of the loan outstanding, which is $150,000. For many middle-class Americans, home equity is their single greatest financial asset. The total value of all home equity held by U.S. households was $23.6 trillion as of the middle of 2021, according to Federal Reserve data.
p195.zh: 家庭还可以通过购买有形资产,特别是住房,寻求回报率。约三分之二的美国家庭拥有自己的家园.房主在房屋中的股本是房主出售房屋并偿还他们用来购买房屋的未偿银行贷款之后的货币价值。 例如,想象一下你以20万美元买房子,支付10%的价格作为定金,并拿出银行贷款来支付剩余的18万美元.随着时间的推移,你还清了一些银行贷款,这样只留下10万美元,房子在市场上的价值上升到25万美元.此时,您在家中的股本是房屋价值减去未偿贷款价值,即15万元. 对于许多中产阶级美国人来说,房屋股权是他们最大的单一金融资产. 根据美联储的数据,截至2021年中,美国家庭持有的所有房屋股本的总价值为23.6万亿美元.

p196.original: Investment in a house is tangibly different from bank accounts, stocks, and bonds because a house offers both a financial and a nonfinancial return. If you buy a house to live in, part of the return on your investment occurs from your consumption of “housing services”—that is, having a place to live. (Of course, if you buy a home and rent it out, you receive rental payments for the housing services you provide, which would offer a financial return.) Buying a house to live in also offers the possibility of a capital gain from selling the house in the future for more than you paid for it. There can, however, be different outcomes, as the Clear It Up on the housing market shows.
p196.zh: 住房投资与银行账户、股票和债券明显不同,因为住房既能带来财务回报,又能带来非财务回报。 如果你买房子居住,你投资的部分收益来自于你对“住房服务”的消费,即拥有居住场所。(当然,如果你买房子并租出去,你就能得到你所提供的住房服务的租金,这可以提供经济回报。 )买房子来住也有可能在未来出售房子获得比付的更多的资本收益。 然而,正如住房市场 " 清查 " 所显示的,可能会有不同的结果。

p197.original: Housing prices have usually risen steadily over time. For example, the median sales price for an existing one-family home was $122,900 in 1990, but 232,000 at the end of December 2016, according to FRED® Economic Data. Over these 24 years, home prices increased an average of 3.1% per year, which is an average financial return over this time.  shows U.S. Census data for the average sales price of a new home in the United States from 1965 to 2021.
p197.zh: 住房价格通常随时间推移而稳步上升。 例如,根据FREDX经济数据,现有一家家庭的中间销售价格在1990年为122 900美元,但在2016年12月底为232 000美元。 在这24年里,房价平均每年上涨3.1%,这是这段时期的平均财政回报. . US.1965年至2021年美国新住宅平均销售价格的人口普查数据.

p198.original: Go to this website to experiment with a compound annual growth rate calculator.
p198.zh: 前往这个网站实验一个复合年增长率计算器.

p199.original: However, the possible capital gains from rising housing prices are riskier than these national price averages. Certain regions of the country or metropolitan areas have seen drops in housing prices over time. The median housing price for the United States as a whole fell almost 7% in 2008 and again in 2009, dropping the median price from $247,900 to $216,700. As of 2016, home values had recovered and even exceeded their pre-recession levels, and they have continued to increase into the early 2020s.
p199.zh: 然而,住房价格上涨可能带来的资本收益比这些国家平均价格的风险更大。国内某些地区或大都会地区住房价格随时间推移而下降。2008年和2009年,美国整体住房价格中位数下跌了近7%,中间价从247,900美元降至216,700美元。 截至2016年,家庭价值已经恢复甚至超过了降级前的水平,并且持续上升至2020年代初期.
